items.prompt: A team says "we changed the database schema but didn't touch the API contract." What does that most likely mean?
choices: They restructured the internal database, but the request/response shape clients see is unchanged
They forgot to update their internal documentation, but clients were still affected by the change
The API is now faster, because the database schema change removed some redundant joins
Clients will need to update their code, since the contract technically changed underneath
items.explanation: The API contract is about what a client can observe and depend on — field names, types, required/optional, endpoint shape. Internal implementation, including the database schema, is free to change as long as the observable contract stays the same.
items.reflection: The line between "contract" and "implementation detail" isn't unique to APIs — a CLI's flag names, a config file's keys, a library's public function signatures all become promises the moment something else is built against them, even if nobody wrote that down. Where in your own work is an "internal detail" actually something another team, script, or future-you already depends on?

items.prompt: Where does an API's contract actually "live," in the sense that matters for deciding whether a change is safe?
choices: In the currently-deployed clients' assumptions about the response shape, not just in a design doc
Only in the OpenAPI/GraphQL schema file in the repo, since that's the single source of truth
In the server's internal code comments, which developers keep in sync with every endpoint change
It doesn't live anywhere until a client complains, so there's no way to know a change is unsafe
items.explanation: A design doc or schema file describes the contract, but what actually determines whether a change is safe is what deployed clients rely on right now — a doc can be technically accurate and a change can still break real traffic if clients depend on something the doc never mentioned.
items.reflection: The line between "contract" and "implementation detail" isn't unique to APIs — a CLI's flag names, a config file's keys, a library's public function signatures all become promises the moment something else is built against them, even if nobody wrote that down. Where in your own work is an "internal detail" actually something another team, script, or future-you already depends on?

items.prompt: A design doc states a signup field phone is required, but the server has in practice always accepted requests that omit it. A new deploy starts rejecting requests without phone, matching the doc exactly. Did this break the contract?
choices: Yes — the real contract is what deployed clients could actually rely on, not what the doc says, and clients omitting phone just lost compatibility
No — the deploy brought the server in line with its own documentation, so nothing was ever actually promised
No — required fields can be enforced at any time without being a contract change
Yes, but only if the doc was written after the server was already in production
items.explanation: The contract is defined by what's actually observable and reliable in production, not by what a doc claims. If clients were, in practice, able to omit the field and succeed, that behavior was part of the real contract — "matching the docs" doesn't make tightening that behavior safe.
items.reflection: The line between "contract" and "implementation detail" isn't unique to APIs — a CLI's flag names, a config file's keys, a library's public function signatures all become promises the moment something else is built against them, even if nobody wrote that down. Where in your own work is an "internal detail" actually something another team, script, or future-you already depends on?

items.prompt: Which of these counts as part of an API's contract with its clients?
choices: Field names, their types, and whether each is required or optional
Which programming language the server is written in internally
How the server's code is organized into files and modules
The name of the internal function that handles the request logic
items.explanation: The contract is exactly the observable request/response shape. Everything about how the server is implemented internally is invisible to clients and free to change.

items.prompt: A server swaps its internal caching library but every response field, type, and status code stays identical. Does this break the API contract?
choices: No — nothing a client can observe changed
Yes — any internal change is automatically a contract change
Only if the cache made responses faster before
Only if the caching library was deprecated
items.explanation: Clients can only depend on what they can observe — field shapes, types, status codes. An internal library swap with zero observable difference can't break anything a client relies on.

items.prompt: Does an API's contract include which HTTP status codes an endpoint can return?
choices: Yes — clients often branch on status codes, so that behavior is part of what they depend on
No — status codes are an HTTP-layer detail, not part of the API contract
Only for 4xx codes, never for 2xx or 5xx
Only if the API documentation explicitly lists every status code
items.explanation: Clients commonly write logic like "if 404, show not-found; if 200, parse the body" — that's a real dependency on status-code behavior, which makes it part of the contract just as much as field shapes.

items.prompt: A team migrates their server from Node.js to Go but keeps every endpoint's request/response shape identical. Is the API contract broken?
choices: No — the implementation language is invisible to clients
Yes — changing languages always changes behavior
Only if the new server is slower
Only if Go serializes JSON differently than Node.js
items.explanation: Clients never see what language a server is written in — only the request/response shape it produces. As long as that shape is unchanged, the contract holds regardless of the implementation underneath.

items.prompt: True or false: a field being "required" or "optional" is part of what a client can depend on.
choices: True — a client that omits an optional field expects success, and relies on that
False — required/optional is purely a server-side validation detail
True, but only for request bodies, never for response fields
False, because validation rules can change at any time without consequence
items.explanation: A client that's used to omitting an optional field is relying on that field staying optional — flipping it to required breaks exactly that client, which is why required/optional status is part of the contract.

items.prompt: Which best describes where an API's contract actually lives, for the purpose of judging whether a change is safe?
choices: In what currently-deployed clients actually assume and depend on
In whatever the most recent engineering design doc says
In the git commit history of the schema file
In whatever the API's marketing page advertises
items.explanation: A design doc describes intent, but the thing that actually gets broken by an unsafe change is real, deployed client code — that's the practical location of "the contract."

items.prompt: A client library's internal variable names are renamed during a refactor, with no change to any network request or response. Does this affect the API contract?
choices: No — internal variable names inside a client are not part of the API contract at all
Yes — any rename anywhere in the system is a contract change
Only if the variables were documented publicly
Only if the client is also the one hosting the API
items.explanation: The API contract is about the request/response shape exchanged over the network. A client's internal variable naming is invisible to the server and to every other client, so it's simply outside the contract's scope.

items.prompt: A server renames a response field from userName to username (lowercase n). Is this breaking?
choices: Yes — any client reading userName now gets undefined
No — it's just a casing fix, so clients won't even notice
Only if the client uses TypeScript, which catches the rename
Only if the field was required, since optional fields don't matter
items.explanation: A rename is functionally identical to removing the old field and adding a new one — from an existing client's point of view, the field it reads is simply gone. Looking like a small cosmetic change doesn't change that.
items.reflection: The breaking/non-breaking test — "does an existing, unmodified caller keep working?" — applies far beyond APIs: a function signature in a shared library, a message format on a queue, even a spreadsheet template other people's formulas reference. Where else have you seen a change that felt like "just a cleanup" actually tighten a promise someone else was relying on?

items.prompt: A server adds a new optional discountPercent field to an existing order response, alongside all the fields already there. Is this breaking?
choices: No — old clients that don't read the new field are unaffected
Yes — any new field changes the response shape clients receive
Only if discountPercent is a number instead of a string
Yes — because the response got larger and slower to parse
items.explanation: Old clients only read the fields they know about; a field they never look for being present alongside the ones they do read has no effect on them. This is the additive, non-breaking half of API evolution.
items.reflection: The breaking/non-breaking test — "does an existing, unmodified caller keep working?" — applies far beyond APIs: a function signature in a shared library, a message format on a queue, even a spreadsheet template other people's formulas reference. Where else have you seen a change that felt like "just a cleanup" actually tighten a promise someone else was relying on?

items.prompt: A server changes a previously-optional shippingAddress field to be required on every order-creation request, and separately adds a brand-new optional giftNote field in the same release. Which part of this release is breaking?
choices: Only the shippingAddress change — making it required rejects requests that used to succeed; giftNote is purely additive and safe on its own
Neither — both changes ship in the same release, so they cancel out
Only giftNote, since any brand-new field is inherently riskier than an existing one
Both — any release that touches more than one field at once is breaking by definition
items.explanation: Each change has to be judged on its own: tightening shippingAddress from optional to required rejects old clients that legitimately omitted it, which is breaking. Adding giftNote as optional is additive and harmless on its own — bundling a safe change alongside an unsafe one doesn't make the safe one unsafe, and it doesn't make the unsafe one safe either.
items.reflection: The breaking/non-breaking test — "does an existing, unmodified caller keep working?" — applies far beyond APIs: a function signature in a shared library, a message format on a queue, even a spreadsheet template other people's formulas reference. Where else have you seen a change that felt like "just a cleanup" actually tighten a promise someone else was relying on?

items.prompt: A server adds a new optional field to a response that no existing client reads. Is this breaking?
choices: No — old clients ignore fields they don't read
Yes — any response shape change is breaking
Only if the new field is required
Only if the field has the same name as an existing one
items.explanation: A client can only be affected by data it actually reads. An additional field nobody was looking for is invisible to every existing client.

items.prompt: A server removes a field named legacyId that it's confirmed zero clients have read in six months of logs. Is removing it breaking?
choices: In principle it's still a removal — but with confirmed zero usage, no currently-deployed client is actually affected
No, because removals are never breaking
Yes, because any removal is automatically catastrophic regardless of usage
No, because the field was named "legacy"
items.explanation: Breaking-ness is about whether a real client is affected, not just the category of change. A field confirmed unused is a case where the category (removal) is normally unsafe, but verified-zero usage means nothing currently depends on it.

items.prompt: A field's type changes from a number to a string in a response (e.g. age: 30 becomes age: "30"). Is this breaking?
choices: Yes — old parsing or validation logic built for a number can fail or misbehave on a string
No — "30" and 30 represent the same value
Only if the client is written in a strictly-typed language
No — type changes only matter for request bodies, not responses
items.explanation: Code written against one type (e.g. doing arithmetic on a number) doesn't automatically work against another type (a string). A type change silently breaks assumptions baked into old client code.

items.prompt: A previously-required field is changed to optional, and the server fills in a sensible default when it's missing. Is this breaking?
choices: No — loosening a constraint can't reject a request that used to succeed
Yes — any change to required/optional status is breaking
Only if the default value is wrong
Yes, because clients now have to check for a missing field they never had to check for
items.explanation: Old clients always sent the field, so they're entirely unaffected by it becoming optional — nothing about their existing behavior stops working. Only the opposite direction, optional becoming required, can reject a previously-valid request.

items.prompt: A new endpoint GET /users/:id/preferences is added. Can this break any existing client?
choices: No — nothing existed at that URL before, so nothing could have depended on it
Yes — new endpoints always risk colliding with existing routes
Only if the new endpoint is slower than existing ones
Yes, because every new endpoint increases the attack surface for every client
items.explanation: A client can only be broken by a change to something it actually depends on. Since the endpoint didn't exist before, there's nothing for an existing client to have built a dependency on.

items.prompt: A default value for an existing, optional sortOrder parameter changes from "asc" to "desc" when the parameter is omitted. Is this breaking?
choices: Yes — clients that relied on the old default now silently get different results
No — the parameter is still optional, so nothing changed
No, because sortOrder doesn't affect which records are returned, only their order
Only if the client explicitly passed sortOrder=asc before
items.explanation: A client that never set the parameter was implicitly relying on the old default behavior. Changing what "doing nothing" produces is a behavior change those clients can't opt out of — that's breaking even though the field itself stayed optional.

items.prompt: A field is renamed, but the old name is kept as an additional alias returning the exact same value, alongside the new name. Is this breaking?
choices: No — old clients reading the old name still get the same value they always got
Yes — any rename is breaking regardless of what else is added
Only if the alias is removed later
Yes, because having two names for the same value is confusing
items.explanation: The test is whether an existing client's behavior changes. Since the old field name still resolves to the same value, nothing an old client depends on actually changed — keeping an alias is exactly how a rename can be made non-breaking.

items.prompt: In REST, what typically identifies a resource and how you can act on it?
choices: A URL (the noun) combined with an HTTP verb (the action)
A single query string naming the fields the client wants back
A GraphQL type definition describing the resource's shape
The response's Content-Type header alone determines this
items.explanation: REST's core idea is resources as nouns (URLs like /users/42) manipulated through a small, fixed set of verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) — the URL + verb pair is what identifies the operation.
items.reflection: REST and GraphQL are two different answers to the same question — "what exactly can a client count on?" — expressed as fixed endpoints versus a queryable schema. The same tension (fixed shape chosen upfront vs. caller picks exactly what it needs) shows up in database views vs. ad-hoc queries, or a report template vs. a spreadsheet pivot table. Where have you seen that same trade-off outside of APIs?

items.prompt: In GraphQL, what determines the shape of a response?
choices: Whatever fields the client's query explicitly selects
A fixed shape defined per endpoint, same as in REST
The HTTP verb used to send the request
The order fields were originally added to the schema
items.explanation: GraphQL inverts REST's fixed-shape-per-endpoint model — the schema defines everything that's queryable, but the actual response shape on any given call is determined by which fields that specific query selected.
items.reflection: REST and GraphQL are two different answers to the same question — "what exactly can a client count on?" — expressed as fixed endpoints versus a queryable schema. The same tension (fixed shape chosen upfront vs. caller picks exactly what it needs) shows up in database views vs. ad-hoc queries, or a report template vs. a spreadsheet pivot table. Where have you seen that same trade-off outside of APIs?

items.prompt: A product listing screen needs each product's name and price, but not its full description, reviews, or supplier info. Against a REST GET /products endpoint that always returns the full product object, and against an equivalent GraphQL query, how does each handle this screen's need?
choices: REST over-fetches (sends the full object every time); GraphQL's query can select just name and price, sending only what the screen needs
Both send the exact same amount of data, since the underlying product data is identical either way
REST under-fetches, forcing extra requests for name and price; GraphQL always over-fetches by design
Neither can solve this — fetching a subset of fields is impossible in both REST and GraphQL
items.explanation: A GraphQL query naming only name and price gets exactly that back, no matter how large the full product object is. A REST endpoint with one fixed shape per resource has no such mechanism — every caller gets the same full object, which is over-fetching for any screen that needs less than everything.
items.reflection: REST and GraphQL are two different answers to the same question — "what exactly can a client count on?" — expressed as fixed endpoints versus a queryable schema. The same tension (fixed shape chosen upfront vs. caller picks exactly what it needs) shows up in database views vs. ad-hoc queries, or a report template vs. a spreadsheet pivot table. Where have you seen that same trade-off outside of APIs?

items.prompt: A REST endpoint GET /users/42 always returns the full user object, even if a screen only needs the user's name. What is this an example of?
choices: Over-fetching — the response includes more than the client needs
Under-fetching — the response is missing data the screen needs
A breaking change in how the endpoint responds to clients
A required-field violation in the response schema
items.explanation: Over-fetching is receiving more data than needed because the endpoint's shape is fixed rather than selectable.

items.prompt: In GraphQL, can two different clients send two different queries to the exact same endpoint and get two differently-shaped responses?
choices: Yes — each query selects its own fields, so the response shape follows the query, not the endpoint
No — GraphQL still returns one fixed shape per endpoint, like REST
Only if the clients use different HTTP verbs
Only if one client is authenticated and the other isn't
items.explanation: There's a single GraphQL endpoint, but each request's response shape is entirely determined by which fields that specific query asked for — two different queries legitimately get two different shapes back.

items.prompt: Does REST require a different URL for every distinct resource (e.g. /users/:id vs /orders/:id)?
choices: Yes — resources are typically identified by distinct URLs, one per resource type/instance
No — REST uses a single endpoint for every resource, same as GraphQL
Only for write operations (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), not for GET
Only if the resources belong to different databases
items.explanation: REST's resource-as-noun model ties each kind of resource (and often each instance) to its own URL, which is part of why adding a new way to fetch data in REST often means adding a new endpoint.

items.prompt: A mobile app screen needs a user, their 5 most recent orders, and each order's line items. Built against a REST API with one endpoint per resource type, what commonly happens?
choices: A waterfall of multiple sequential requests — one for the user, then one per order, then one per order's line items
A single request automatically returns everything nested, the same as GraphQL would
The request fails, since REST cannot represent nested data under any circumstance
The server merges all three resources into one response automatically, without any extra endpoint work
items.explanation: Without a purpose-built endpoint for this exact combination, the client has to fetch pieces separately and loop — that's the N+1 waterfall pattern that a single nested GraphQL query avoids.

items.prompt: What does it mean for an HTTP verb like DELETE to express "the action" in REST's URL + verb model?
choices: The verb says what to do to the resource the URL names — DELETE /orders/9 means "delete order 9"
The verb only affects how fast the request is processed, not what happens
The verb is purely cosmetic and has no effect on server behavior
The verb determines which database the request is routed to
items.explanation: REST pairs a noun (the URL, naming a resource) with a verb (the HTTP method, naming the action) — DELETE /orders/9 reads directly as "delete this specific order," which is the core of REST's design.

items.prompt: Can a GraphQL query ask for deeply nested data (e.g. a user, their orders, and each order's line items) in a single request?
choices: Yes — that's exactly what GraphQL's nested field selection is designed for
No — GraphQL can only return flat, single-level objects
Only if each nesting level has its own dedicated GraphQL endpoint
Only for read operations, never for mutations
items.explanation: GraphQL queries can select nested fields to arbitrary depth in one request — user { orders { lineItems { ... } } } — which is exactly what avoids REST's N+1 waterfall for the same data.

items.prompt: Under-fetching, as distinct from over-fetching, refers to what kind of problem?
choices: A single response doesn't contain enough nested/related data, forcing additional requests to get the rest
A response contains more fields than the client actually needed
A request is missing a required field and gets rejected
A response arrives with the wrong Content-Type header
items.explanation: Under-fetching is the mirror problem to over-fetching: instead of getting too much in one response, the client doesn't get enough and has to make further requests to assemble what it actually needs.

items.prompt: What does API versioning fundamentally let a team do that they couldn't do otherwise?
choices: Run an old and a new contract at the same time, so existing clients keep working during a transition
Avoid ever making a breaking change, since versioning prevents them entirely
Skip writing tests for new features while the old version is maintained
Automatically update every client's code to the new contract's shape
items.explanation: Versioning doesn't prevent breaking changes — it lets two contracts coexist so clients on the old one keep working while new clients (or an eventual forced migration) move to the new one. It's a transition mechanism, not a way to avoid change.
items.reflection: Versioning is really a transition tool, not a wall against change — the same idea shows up in feature flags, database migrations that keep reading both an old and new column during a rollout, or a company running two pricing plans side by side while customers migrate off the old one. Where else have you seen "run both, on purpose, for a while" used to avoid forcing everyone to move at once?

items.prompt: Why not just ship a breaking change directly, without any version, and let clients update whenever they notice?
choices: Some clients (old app installs, unattended integrations) can't update on the server's schedule, so they'd simply break
HTTP doesn't allow breaking changes without a version negotiation header
Breaking changes are always illegal in production APIs by convention
Clients automatically retry until they get the new shape they expect
items.explanation: Not every client can upgrade the moment the server changes — a mobile app install can't force-update overnight, and an unattended integration might not notice a change for months. Versioning exists precisely because "just tell clients to update" isn't realistic on the server's timeline.
items.reflection: Versioning is really a transition tool, not a wall against change — the same idea shows up in feature flags, database migrations that keep reading both an old and new column during a rollout, or a company running two pricing plans side by side while customers migrate off the old one. Where else have you seen "run both, on purpose, for a while" used to avoid forcing everyone to move at once?

items.prompt: A team ships /v2 alongside /v1, then never revisits the decision again — three years later, both versions are still fully maintained, and nobody is sure how many clients still use /v1. What does this scenario reveal about what versioning actually buys a team?
choices: Versioning buys time for a transition, but only if the team actively manages and eventually completes that transition — left unmanaged, it becomes a permanent maintenance burden instead of a temporary bridge
This is the correct, intended end state of versioning — supported versions should accumulate indefinitely as a permanent safety net
This proves versioning doesn't work and breaking changes should simply be shipped without warning instead
This is only a problem if /v1 and /v2 share no code — sharing a core logic layer makes indefinite dual-support free
items.explanation: Versioning is only valuable as a bridge to an eventual single contract again — every supported version is ongoing work (testing, documentation, bug-fixing) someone has to keep doing. Without the monitoring-and-removal steps L2/L3 cover, "temporary" dual support quietly becomes permanent, which defeats the entire point: versioning was meant to buy time, not replace the decision to eventually finish the migration.
items.reflection: Versioning is really a transition tool, not a wall against change — the same idea shows up in feature flags, database migrations that keep reading both an old and new column during a rollout, or a company running two pricing plans side by side while customers migrate off the old one. Where else have you seen "run both, on purpose, for a while" used to avoid forcing everyone to move at once?

items.prompt: Does versioning an API prevent breaking changes from ever happening?
choices: No — it lets an old and new contract run side by side so clients aren't forced to update instantly
Yes — that's the entire purpose of versioning
Only for GraphQL APIs, not REST ones
Only if the version number is incremented by more than one
items.explanation: Versioning doesn't stop breaking changes from happening — it changes how clients experience them, by giving old clients time on the old contract while the new one rolls out.

items.prompt: A mobile app can't force every installed copy to update the moment a server changes. Why does this matter for API versioning?
choices: It's exactly why versioning exists — old installs need a contract that keeps working until they eventually update
It doesn't matter, since app stores update every device automatically and instantly
It only matters for Android, not iOS
It only matters if the app has more than a million installs
items.explanation: Old app installs are a textbook case of a client that can't move at the server's pace — versioning exists specifically to let those installs keep working on the old contract.

items.prompt: An unattended integration script hasn't been touched by its owner in a year. If the API it calls ships a breaking change with no version, what happens?
choices: The script breaks, since nobody is monitoring it to react to the change
The script automatically adapts, since most integrations include error-correction logic
Nothing, since unattended scripts are immune to API changes
The API provider is legally required to fix the script
items.explanation: An unattended, unmonitored integration has no way to react to a change it doesn't even know happened — this is exactly the kind of client versioning is meant to protect by keeping the old contract alive.

items.prompt: Is a supported API version meant to be maintained forever once it's shipped?
choices: No — it's meant to be a temporary bridge until clients migrate, then retired
Yes — every version a team ever ships should stay supported indefinitely
Only major versions are temporary; minor versions are permanent
Only if the version has fewer than 1,000 active clients
items.explanation: A version is a promise with an expiration date, not a permanent fork — every version still open is ongoing work, which is why eventually completing the migration and retiring it matters.

items.prompt: What's the main cost of supporting multiple API versions at once?
choices: Every supported version is ongoing work — testing, documentation, and bug-fixing all have to continue for it
There is no real cost, since old versions require zero maintenance
The only cost is a slightly longer URL for versioned endpoints
The cost is paid entirely by clients, never by the API's own team
items.explanation: Each version a team keeps running still needs tests, docs, and fixes kept current — that ongoing cost is exactly why versioning is meant to be temporary, not a permanent arrangement.

items.prompt: A third-party integration partner explicitly asks for 90 days' notice before any breaking change. What does versioning let the API team do in response?
choices: Ship the new contract as a new version immediately, while keeping the old version live for at least those 90 days
Tell the partner breaking changes can't be scheduled or announced in advance
Force the partner to rewrite their integration within 24 hours regardless
Ignore the request, since versioning only applies to internal clients
items.explanation: Versioning is exactly the mechanism that makes a notice period like this honorable — the old version keeps working unmodified for however long the transition needs, while the new version is already available.

items.prompt: True or false: versioning is best understood as a way to avoid ever having to make a breaking change.
choices: False — it's a way to manage a breaking change that's already decided, by letting both contracts coexist for a while
True — a well-versioned API never actually breaks anything
True, but only if the API uses GraphQL
False, because versioning actually causes breaking changes rather than managing them
items.explanation: Versioning doesn't make a breaking change go away — it manages the transition around a breaking change that's already necessary, giving existing clients time instead of forcing an instant cutover.

items.prompt: In the shared-core-plus-adapters pattern, why do /v1 and /v2 both call the same underlying function instead of having separate implementations?
choices: So a bug fix or business-logic change only needs to be made in one place
Because REST requires every versioned endpoint to share one implementation
To make the API slower on purpose, trading speed for consistency
Because GraphQL doesn't support this shared-core pattern at all
items.explanation: Forking implementation per version means every future fix or business-rule change has to be applied, tested, and deployed separately for each supported version — and versions can silently drift apart from each other. Routing through one shared core avoids both problems.
items.reflection: Routing every variant through one shared core and keeping only thin edges per-version is the same idea as the "adapter" or "facade" pattern anywhere — a translation layer in front of a legacy system, a device driver exposing one interface over different hardware. Where else have you seen "keep the real logic in one place, vary only the edges" pay off, or seen the opposite (duplicated logic per variant) cause real drift?

items.prompt: A bug is found in how order totals are calculated. In a codebase where /v1 and /v2 are both thin adapters over one shared core function, how many places need the fix?
choices: One — the shared core
Two — once per version
Zero — versions are independent by design
It depends on which version is newer
items.explanation: Because both adapters delegate the actual calculation to the same core function, fixing it there fixes it for every version's adapter simultaneously. This is the entire benefit of the pattern over maintaining separate codebases per version.
items.reflection: Routing every variant through one shared core and keeping only thin edges per-version is the same idea as the "adapter" or "facade" pattern anywhere — a translation layer in front of a legacy system, a device driver exposing one interface over different hardware. Where else have you seen "keep the real logic in one place, vary only the edges" pay off, or seen the opposite (duplicated logic per variant) cause real drift?

items.prompt: A team maintains /v1 and /v2 as two fully separate codebases (no shared core). A security fix is applied to /v2 but the engineer forgets /v1 exists. Six months later, a client on /v1 is compromised by the same vulnerability. What does this scenario demonstrate about the risk of forking implementations per version, and how would a shared-core design have changed the outcome?
choices: It demonstrates exactly the drift risk forking creates — a shared core would have meant the fix landed once, in the one place both versions' adapters call, so /v1 would have picked it up automatically
It demonstrates that versioning itself is unsafe and should never be used, regardless of implementation strategy
It demonstrates that /v1 should simply have been removed earlier, which is unrelated to whether the core was shared
It demonstrates that security fixes should always be applied to the oldest version first, not the newest
items.explanation: This is precisely the failure mode the shared-core pattern exists to prevent: with separate codebases, a fix applied to one doesn't automatically reach the other, and nothing forces anyone to remember both exist. A shared core removes the "remembering" step entirely — the fix lives in the one place every version's adapter calls through, so there's no second codebase to forget.
items.reflection: Routing every variant through one shared core and keeping only thin edges per-version is the same idea as the "adapter" or "facade" pattern anywhere — a translation layer in front of a legacy system, a device driver exposing one interface over different hardware. Where else have you seen "keep the real logic in one place, vary only the edges" pay off, or seen the opposite (duplicated logic per variant) cause real drift?

items.prompt: Why do REST version adapters usually hold as little logic as possible?
choices: So all the real business logic stays in one shared place, and the adapters just reshape input/output
Because adapters are required by the HTTP specification to be stateless
Because thin adapters make requests faster over the network
Because GraphQL requires REST adapters to be thin before it can interoperate
items.explanation: Keeping adapters thin — pure reshaping, no business logic — is what makes the shared-core pattern work: the actual logic exists exactly once, and every version's adapter just translates to/from it.

items.prompt: If /v1 and /v2 both call the same shared getOrderTotal() function, and that function's rounding logic is fixed, which versions see the fix?
choices: Both — since both adapters call the same function, the fix applies to each automatically
Only /v2, since it's the newer version
Neither, until each adapter is redeployed separately
Only /v1, since it was presumably the one with the bug
items.explanation: Because both versions route through the identical shared function, a fix made there is immediately visible to every adapter that calls it — no separate deploy per version needed.

items.prompt: What's the main long-term risk of maintaining a fully separate codebase per API version instead of thin adapters over a shared core?
choices: Versions quietly drift apart as fixes and rules get applied inconsistently across copies
The server becomes faster, since each version has its own dedicated code path
Old versions become impossible to deprecate once they're fully separate
There's no risk — separate codebases are simpler to reason about
items.explanation: Every fix, security patch, or business-rule change now has to be remembered and reapplied in N places. In practice this drifts — some versions get a fix, others are forgotten — until versions behave inconsistently in ways nobody intended.

items.prompt: In the shared-core pattern, what is a version's "adapter" responsible for?
choices: Reshaping the shared core's input/output to match that version's specific contract shape
Storing a separate copy of the business logic for that version only
Deciding which database table the request should query
Authenticating the client before any request reaches the core
items.explanation: The adapter's whole job is translation at the edge — taking the core's version-agnostic result and reshaping it into whatever JSON shape that particular version promises, nothing more.

items.prompt: A team adds a brand-new /v3 adapter that also calls the existing shared core function, unchanged. Does the core need to know /v3 exists?
choices: No — the core is version-agnostic; only the new /v3 adapter needs to know how to reshape its output
Yes — every version must be hardcoded into the core's logic
Yes, but only if /v3 adds new required fields
No, but only if /v3 is identical in shape to /v2
items.explanation: The entire point of a version-agnostic core is that it never needs to change just because a new version's adapter is added on top of it — that's what keeps adding a version cheap.

items.prompt: Two versions, /v1 and /v2, each hold their own full copy of the validation logic for a signup form. A new validation rule is added only to /v2's copy. What's the resulting risk?
choices: /v1 and /v2 can now silently enforce different rules on the same kind of request, which is exactly the drift a shared core prevents
No risk — versions are supposed to behave completely independently of each other
The risk only matters if /v1 is the newer version
This is actually the correct and expected behavior for any versioned API
items.explanation: Duplicated logic per version means a change applied to only one copy creates real, often unintended, behavioral divergence between versions — the exact problem a shared core, with thin per-version adapters, is designed to avoid.

items.prompt: Why is it specifically the "shared core," and not the adapters, where persistence/database logic should live?
choices: Because persistence is business logic that every version needs identically — duplicating it per adapter risks the same drift as duplicating any other rule
Because adapters are not allowed to make database calls under any circumstances
Because the database schema itself depends on which API version is calling it
Because persistence logic is unrelated to the question of versioning at all
items.explanation: Persistence is exactly the kind of logic that must behave identically regardless of which version's adapter triggered it — keeping it in the shared core, rather than duplicating it per adapter, is what the pattern is built around.

items.prompt: Does marking a GraphQL field @deprecated stop it from resolving when an old client queries it?
choices: No — the resolver still runs and returns real data until the field is actually removed
Yes — it immediately returns null to signal the field is going away
Yes — the query fails with an error pointing at the deprecated field
It depends on the GraphQL server version and its configuration
items.explanation: @deprecated is metadata for tooling (IDE warnings, introspection, codegen) — it doesn't change runtime behavior at all. The field's resolver keeps executing normally until someone deletes the field/resolver itself.
items.reflection: @deprecated is a label for intent, not an action — the same gap exists in code comments like // TODO: remove this, or a feature flag left at "50% rollout" for a year: naming an intention doesn't execute it, and skipping the step that actually verifies it's safe to finish is how "temporary" markers become permanent. Where have you seen an announced intention never actually get followed through on?

items.prompt: What is @deprecated primarily useful for?
choices: Surfacing a retirement warning in developer tooling (IDEs, codegen, schema docs) without breaking anyone yet
Automatically migrating old clients to the new field without any code changes
Blocking new clients from ever querying the old, deprecated field
Reducing the field's response size once it's marked for removal
items.explanation: It's a signal aimed at developers building against the schema — it shows up as a warning in tooling — while leaving the field fully functional for whoever is still using it. It communicates intent to remove later, nothing more.
items.reflection: @deprecated is a label for intent, not an action — the same gap exists in code comments like // TODO: remove this, or a feature flag left at "50% rollout" for a year: naming an intention doesn't execute it, and skipping the step that actually verifies it's safe to finish is how "temporary" markers become permanent. Where have you seen an announced intention never actually get followed through on?

items.prompt: A field is marked @deprecated on Monday. On Tuesday, a teammate deletes its resolver function, reasoning "it's already deprecated, so it's basically gone anyway." What actually happens on Tuesday, and what step did the teammate skip?
choices: Every client still querying that field breaks immediately in production on Tuesday; the teammate skipped verifying real usage had actually dropped to zero before removing it
Nothing happens, since @deprecated already disabled the field on Monday
Only new clients are affected; existing clients keep working because they cached the old schema
The field keeps working exactly as before, since deleting a resolver has no runtime effect in GraphQL
items.explanation: @deprecated never changed runtime behavior — the field was fully live the entire time between Monday and Tuesday. Deleting the resolver is the actual removal, and doing it without checking real usage first treats the announcement as if it were already the completed migration, which it wasn't.
items.reflection: @deprecated is a label for intent, not an action — the same gap exists in code comments like // TODO: remove this, or a feature flag left at "50% rollout" for a year: naming an intention doesn't execute it, and skipping the step that actually verifies it's safe to finish is how "temporary" markers become permanent. Where have you seen an announced intention never actually get followed through on?

items.prompt: After a field is marked @deprecated, does a query that still selects it succeed or fail?
choices: It succeeds — the field still resolves normally
It fails with a schema validation error
It succeeds but always returns null
It depends on whether the client is using a GraphQL IDE
items.explanation: @deprecated doesn't change what the server does at runtime — the query still succeeds and the field still resolves to a real value.

items.prompt: Where does a @deprecated warning typically show up for a developer working with the schema?
choices: In IDE autocomplete/warnings, schema introspection tools, and codegen output
As an HTTP 410 Gone status on every request
In the response body itself, as an extra warning field
Nowhere — @deprecated has no visible effect anywhere
items.explanation: @deprecated metadata is surfaced through developer tooling — IDE hints, introspection queries, codegen warnings — which is exactly how a developer building against the schema finds out a field is on its way out.

items.prompt: Is it safe to delete a deprecated field's resolver the moment @deprecated is added?
choices: No — deleting the resolver is the actual removal and will break any client still using it
Yes — that's the entire purpose of the @deprecated directive
Yes, but only for fields of type Float
No, but only because GraphQL technically disallows deleting resolvers
items.explanation: Adding @deprecated only announces intent — it doesn't mean usage has actually dropped to zero. Deleting the resolver immediately after is the real removal step, and doing it without checking usage risks breaking real clients.

items.prompt: A deprecated field's resolver keeps being called by old clients for months after @deprecated was added. Is this expected?
choices: Yes — @deprecated only warns; the field keeps working for as long as any client queries it
No — the field should have stopped resolving the day it was marked
No, this means the @deprecated directive was applied incorrectly
Yes, but only if the field returns a scalar type
items.explanation: This is exactly the expected behavior — deprecation doesn't shut a field off, so any client still querying it keeps getting real, correct data until someone actually removes the field.

items.prompt: Can a new client query a field that's marked @deprecated, the same way an old client does?
choices: Yes — the field is still a normal, fully functional part of the schema until it's actually removed
No — @deprecated blocks any client that wasn't already using the field before the mark was added
Only if the new client ignores the deprecation warning in its tooling
No — deprecated fields are only visible to clients on the oldest schema version
items.explanation: @deprecated doesn't restrict who can query a field — any client, old or new, gets the exact same working field. The directive only discourages new usage through tooling warnings, it doesn't enforce anything at runtime.

items.prompt: What should happen before a deprecated field's resolver is actually deleted?
choices: Real usage of the field should be confirmed to have dropped to zero (or a sunset date reached with that confirmed)
Nothing — deletion can happen the moment @deprecated is added, with no further checks
The field should first be renamed, then deleted a week later
The field's type should be changed to nullable before deletion
items.explanation: Skipping a usage check before deletion is exactly how "should be safe to remove" turns into a real outage — confirming usage is actually gone is what makes the eventual removal genuinely safe.

items.prompt: True or false: @deprecated changes the response a query gets back for that field.
choices: False — the response is unaffected; only tooling-facing metadata changes
True — the field's value is replaced with a deprecation notice string
True, but only in GraphQL servers written in Node.js
False, because @deprecated can only be applied to mutations, not queries
items.explanation: The actual data returned for the field is completely unaffected by @deprecated — it's a schema-level annotation read by tooling, not something that alters runtime responses.

items.prompt: Which of these is a common place a REST API's version lives?
choices: The URL path, e.g. /v2/users
Inside the response body's first field
The HTTP method used
The client's User-Agent string
items.explanation: URL-path versioning (/v1/, /v2/) and a versioned Accept/media-type header are the two most common places REST carries a version — both are part of the request itself, visible before the server even processes the body.
items.reflection: Carrying a version as visible, structural information (a URL segment) versus as metadata (a header) is a choice that shows up well beyond APIs — a file extension vs. a MIME type, a URL slug vs. a cookie for a site's A/B test variant. Where have you seen "put it in the visible path" versus "put it in the invisible metadata" trade off differently for discoverability vs. flexibility?

items.prompt: Does a typical GraphQL API put a version number in its endpoint URL the way REST does?
choices: No — GraphQL usually has a single endpoint and evolves one schema additively instead
Yes — /graphql/v1, /graphql/v2 is the standard versioning pattern
Only for mutations, not queries, which never need a version
Yes, but only for breaking changes to scalar types specifically
items.explanation: GraphQL's usual design keeps one endpoint and one schema; instead of standing up a parallel URL per version, it adds new fields/types and deprecates retiring ones. There's no second deployment to route between — deprecation is schema metadata, not a fork.
items.reflection: Carrying a version as visible, structural information (a URL segment) versus as metadata (a header) is a choice that shows up well beyond APIs — a file extension vs. a MIME type, a URL slug vs. a cookie for a site's A/B test variant. Where have you seen "put it in the visible path" versus "put it in the invisible metadata" trade off differently for discoverability vs. flexibility?

items.prompt: A team is choosing between putting a REST API's version in the URL path (/v2/users) versus in an Accept header (Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json). A junior engineer argues "URL is simpler, let's always use that." What's a real consideration that could favor the header approach instead, and does that make URL versioning wrong?
choices: A header lets the same URL serve multiple versions via content negotiation, which matters for caching/bookmarking a stable URL across versions — but URL versioning is still valid; it's a trade-off, not a correctness issue
URL versioning is objectively wrong in all cases, since REST specifications mandate header-based versioning
There's no real difference — both approaches are functionally and practically identical in every situation
Header versioning is always worse because headers can't be seen in a browser's address bar
items.explanation: Both are legitimate, commonly-used strategies with different trade-offs: URL versioning is visible and simple to reason about (and to route on), while header versioning keeps one stable URL and negotiates the version via metadata, which can matter for caching or bookmarking behavior. Neither is a correctness requirement — it's a design trade-off a team makes deliberately.
items.reflection: Carrying a version as visible, structural information (a URL segment) versus as metadata (a header) is a choice that shows up well beyond APIs — a file extension vs. a MIME type, a URL slug vs. a cookie for a site's A/B test variant. Where have you seen "put it in the visible path" versus "put it in the invisible metadata" trade off differently for discoverability vs. flexibility?

items.prompt: Where is a version typically placed in URL-path versioning?
choices: As a segment in the path itself, e.g. /v2/users/42
As part of the query string only, e.g. ?v=2
Inside the request body as a JSON field
In the response's status code
items.explanation: URL-path versioning puts the version directly in the path, as a segment like /v1/ or /v2/, making it visible in the URL itself.

items.prompt: What does the Accept header approach to versioning rely on?
choices: Content negotiation — the client states which version's media type it wants in the Accept header
The server guessing the client's version from its IP address
A cookie set on the client's first request
The response's Content-Length header
items.explanation: Header-based versioning uses HTTP content negotiation — the client's Accept header names the specific versioned media type it wants, and the server responds accordingly.

items.prompt: Does GraphQL need a mechanism equivalent to REST's /v1 vs /v2 URLs?
choices: No — its one evolving schema, with fields added and deprecated, serves the same purpose differently
Yes — GraphQL servers always expose multiple endpoints, one per version
Yes, but only when breaking changes affect the root Query type
No, because GraphQL doesn't support breaking changes at all
items.explanation: GraphQL doesn't need parallel URLs because its schema itself evolves additively — new fields coexist with deprecated ones in the same schema, at the same single endpoint.

items.prompt: A client sends a request to /v1/orders. What does this tell the server about which contract to honor?
choices: The URL itself routes the request to the v1 adapter/handler directly
Nothing — the server always serves the latest version regardless of the URL
It tells the server to use GraphQL instead of REST for this request
It only matters if the request also includes an Accept header
items.explanation: With URL-path versioning, the path segment itself is the routing signal — a request to /v1/orders is unambiguously asking for the v1 contract.

items.prompt: Is it possible for a REST API to combine URL versioning with other versioning signals, like a header?
choices: Yes — a team could use both, though most APIs pick one primary mechanism to avoid ambiguity
No — REST APIs are restricted to exactly one versioning mechanism by the HTTP spec
Yes, but only if the API has fewer than two supported versions
No, because headers and URLs can never both be read by the same server
items.explanation: There's no technical restriction against combining mechanisms, but most teams pick one primary approach — using both at once for the same decision risks the two signals disagreeing with each other.

items.prompt: A GraphQL schema adds a new field and deprecates an old one, with no URL change at all. Does a client need to point at a different endpoint to see the new field?
choices: No — the same single endpoint now serves both the old and new field from the same schema
Yes — every schema change requires a new endpoint
Only if the new field has a different return type than the old one
Only if the client is using introspection
items.explanation: Because GraphQL evolves one schema in place, a client querying the exact same endpoint automatically has access to both the newly-added field and the still-working deprecated one — no new URL involved.

items.prompt: What's a practical downside of URL-path versioning that header-based versioning avoids?
choices: Every supported version needs its own set of routes/URLs to maintain and document
URL-path versioning can't be cached by browsers or CDNs at all
URL-path versioning requires a GraphQL schema to function
URL-path versioning is incompatible with HTTPS
items.explanation: Versioning by URL means each version is a literally separate set of routes to keep documented and working, whereas header-based versioning can keep one set of URLs and vary only the negotiated response shape.

items.prompt: A mobile screen needs a user's name and their last order's total — nothing else. Against a REST GET /users/:id that always returns the full user object, what's happening?
choices: Over-fetching — the response includes more than the client needs
Under-fetching — not enough data is returned for this screen's needs
A breaking change occurred in the response shape clients depend on
The endpoint is misconfigured and needs a new deployment
items.explanation: The endpoint's response shape is fixed regardless of what the caller actually needs, so the client always gets the full object — including every field the screen has no use for. GraphQL avoids this by letting the query select just name and the order total.
items.reflection: Over-fetching and under-fetching are really the two failure modes of "one fixed shape has to serve every caller" — the same tension shows up in a one-size report that either drowns some readers in detail or leaves others wanting more, or a single database view that's too wide for some queries and too narrow for others. Where have you had to pick a single fixed shape and felt that trade-off directly?

items.prompt: A screen needs a user, their orders, and each order's line items. Built against a REST API with one endpoint per resource, why does this typically require multiple sequential requests (a waterfall)?
choices: Each REST endpoint returns a fixed shape for one resource type — nested data isn't included unless a specific endpoint is built for that exact combination
REST doesn't support nested data at all, ever, so clients must always fetch pieces separately
The server intentionally throttles requests to limit how much data any client can pull at once
REST always requires authentication per request, which adds a round trip for every nested lookup
items.explanation: Without a purpose-built endpoint for this exact combination, the client has to fetch the user, then loop over orders to fetch each one's line items — an N+1 pattern. GraphQL's single query with nested field selection avoids building a new endpoint for every combination screens need.
items.reflection: Over-fetching and under-fetching are really the two failure modes of "one fixed shape has to serve every caller" — the same tension shows up in a one-size report that either drowns some readers in detail or leaves others wanting more, or a single database view that's too wide for some queries and too narrow for others. Where have you had to pick a single fixed shape and felt that trade-off directly?

items.prompt: A team builds a dedicated REST endpoint, GET /dashboard-summary, that returns exactly the fields three different screens need, combined, to avoid both over- and under-fetching for those specific screens. Six months later a fourth screen needs a slightly different combination. What trade-off did the team make by solving over/under-fetching this way, compared to a GraphQL schema?
choices: They avoided over/under-fetching for the three original screens at the cost of needing a brand-new purpose-built endpoint for every new combination — GraphQL's per-query field selection would have served the fourth screen with no new endpoint
They made no trade-off at all — a purpose-built REST endpoint is strictly equivalent to GraphQL in every respect
This proves REST can never solve over/under-fetching under any circumstances
This proves GraphQL endpoints also need to be purpose-built per screen, just like REST
items.explanation: Building one tailored endpoint does solve the problem for the screens it was designed for — but that solution doesn't generalize: each new combination of needs requires another purpose-built endpoint. GraphQL's per-query field selection solves the same over/under-fetching problem generically, since any new combination is just a different query against the same schema, not a new endpoint to build and maintain.
items.reflection: Over-fetching and under-fetching are really the two failure modes of "one fixed shape has to serve every caller" — the same tension shows up in a one-size report that either drowns some readers in detail or leaves others wanting more, or a single database view that's too wide for some queries and too narrow for others. Where have you had to pick a single fixed shape and felt that trade-off directly?

items.prompt: What is over-fetching?
choices: Receiving more data in a response than the client actually needs
Receiving less data than the client needs, forcing extra requests
A request that fails due to a missing required field
A request that times out due to server load
items.explanation: Over-fetching means a response contains more than what's actually needed — typically because the endpoint's shape is fixed and can't be trimmed per caller.

items.prompt: What is under-fetching?
choices: Not getting enough nested/related data in one response, requiring more requests to get the rest
Getting more fields back than were asked for
A field in the response having the wrong type
A query exceeding the server's rate limit
items.explanation: Under-fetching is the mirror problem to over-fetching — a single response doesn't include enough to satisfy the need, so the client has to make additional round trips.

items.prompt: A GraphQL query selects exactly name and orderTotal and nothing else. Does the server send back any other fields from the User or Order types?
choices: No — only the fields explicitly selected in the query are returned
Yes — GraphQL always returns the full object regardless of the query
Only if those other fields are marked as required in the schema
Only if the client doesn't specify a query at all
items.explanation: GraphQL's response shape is driven entirely by what the query selects — fields not named in the query simply aren't included in the response, avoiding over-fetching by construction.

items.prompt: A REST endpoint GET /orders/:id/line-items has to be fetched separately for every order in a list, one request per order. What problem does this illustrate?
choices: Under-fetching — the initial orders list didn't include enough to avoid these extra, per-order requests
Over-fetching — too much data came back in the initial request
A breaking change in the orders endpoint
A caching failure on the client side
items.explanation: Needing a follow-up request per order because the first response didn't carry what was needed is exactly under-fetching — more requests are forced to assemble the full picture.

items.prompt: Can a single GraphQL query avoid both over-fetching and under-fetching for the same screen?
choices: Yes — by selecting exactly the fields and nested relations that screen needs, no more and no less
No — any single query will always do one or the other
Only if the screen needs fewer than three fields total
Only for queries, never for data involving relationships between types
items.explanation: Because the query names precisely what's needed, including nested relations at whatever depth is required, it can match a screen's actual need exactly — avoiding both extremes at once.

items.prompt: A fixed-shape REST endpoint serves ten different screens, each needing a different subset of its fields. What's the structural reason this tends to produce over-fetching for most of them?
choices: One shape has to be wide enough to cover every screen's needs, so most screens get fields beyond what they individually use
REST endpoints automatically detect which screen is calling and adjust their response
This never produces over-fetching as long as the endpoint returns JSON
It only happens if the endpoint uses the GET method
items.explanation: A single fixed shape serving many different callers has to be a superset of what any one caller needs — which means most individual callers end up receiving fields irrelevant to them.

items.prompt: Does under-fetching only happen with nested/related data, or can it also happen with a single flat resource?
choices: It's most associated with nested/related data, since a flat resource's fixed shape either has a field or it doesn't — missing a field there is more a contract gap than classic under-fetching
It can never happen with nested data, only flat resources
It happens equally often regardless of nesting, with no structural pattern
It only happens when the server returns XML instead of JSON
items.explanation: Under-fetching is most visible with relationships — a user's orders, an order's line items — where a flat, single-resource response simply doesn't carry the next level down, forcing the extra round trip.

items.prompt: In the deprecation flow (ship new -> announce -> monitor usage -> remove), what's the purpose of the monitor-usage step specifically?
choices: To verify real traffic has actually stopped depending on the old field/version before removing it, since not every client will act on an announcement
To measure server response time before and after the deprecation announcement goes out
To decide which team owns the migration once the old field is finally removed
To generate documentation automatically for whichever field is marked next
items.explanation: An announced sunset date is a plan, not proof every caller has moved off the old contract — some are unattended scripts or abandoned integrations that will never see the announcement. Monitoring turns "we announced it" into "we verified it's actually safe" before removal.
items.reflection: "Announce, then verify, then act" instead of "announce, then act" generalizes well past APIs — a company sunsetting an old product line, a team retiring a shared internal tool, even cleaning out a shared drive folder everyone was told about a year ago. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of trusting that an announcement alone meant everyone had actually moved on?

items.prompt: What's the correct order of the deprecation steps: ship the replacement, announce a sunset date, monitor real usage, remove the old field/version?
choices: Ship replacement -> announce sunset date -> monitor usage -> remove
Announce sunset date -> remove -> ship replacement -> monitor usage
Remove -> ship replacement -> announce -> monitor
Monitor usage -> ship replacement -> remove -> announce
items.explanation: The replacement has to exist before anyone can migrate to it; the announcement sets expectations and a target date; monitoring confirms the migration actually happened before the final, irreversible removal step.
items.reflection: "Announce, then verify, then act" instead of "announce, then act" generalizes well past APIs — a company sunsetting an old product line, a team retiring a shared internal tool, even cleaning out a shared drive folder everyone was told about a year ago. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of trusting that an announcement alone meant everyone had actually moved on?

items.prompt: A sunset date for a deprecated field passes. Monitoring shows the field still has nonzero traffic from two integration partners who never responded to outreach. What should happen next, and why is "remove it anyway, the date already passed" the wrong move?
choices: Keep the field live and escalate direct outreach to the remaining callers — removing on schedule despite confirmed nonzero usage would break real, identified traffic, defeating the purpose of monitoring in the first place
Remove it immediately — a sunset date is a hard deadline that overrides any usage data once it passes
Remove it, since two partners is too small a number to matter for a public API
Extend the sunset date by exactly the same amount of time it was originally announced, regardless of what monitoring shows
items.explanation: The sunset date is a target, not a guarantee — the entire reason to monitor usage is to catch exactly this situation, where real traffic hasn't actually migrated yet. Removing on schedule anyway throws away the information monitoring just gave you and breaks identified, still-active callers; the correct move is to use what monitoring revealed (who's still calling) to drive direct follow-up before removal.
items.reflection: "Announce, then verify, then act" instead of "announce, then act" generalizes well past APIs — a company sunsetting an old product line, a team retiring a shared internal tool, even cleaning out a shared drive folder everyone was told about a year ago. Where have you seen (or made) the mistake of trusting that an announcement alone meant everyone had actually moved on?

items.prompt: What's the first step in the deprecation flow, before anything is announced?
choices: Ship the replacement field/version so there's something to migrate to
Announce a sunset date to all known clients
Immediately remove the old field
Monitor usage of a field that hasn't been replaced yet
items.explanation: A replacement has to exist before anyone can be asked to migrate to it — announcing a sunset date for something with no replacement yet gives clients nothing to move to.

items.prompt: Why announce a sunset date instead of just quietly monitoring usage and removing a field whenever it looks safe?
choices: An announced date sets clear expectations and gives client teams a deadline to plan their own migration around
Announcing is purely a legal formality with no practical benefit
Sunset dates are required by the HTTP specification
Announcing is only necessary for GraphQL APIs, not REST
items.explanation: A clear, communicated deadline lets other teams plan their migration work — without one, "eventually" never becomes a real priority on anyone else's schedule.

items.prompt: If monitoring shows a deprecated field's usage has dropped to exactly zero, what's the next appropriate step?
choices: Proceed with removing the field/version
Wait indefinitely regardless of the zero reading, just in case
Immediately re-deprecate a different, unrelated field
Lower the field's priority without taking any further action
items.explanation: Confirmed zero usage is exactly the signal the monitoring step exists to produce — once it's there, removal is the safe next step in the flow.

items.prompt: A team skips the monitor-usage step entirely and removes a deprecated field the day after the sunset date passes. What risk does this create?
choices: Breaking any client that hadn't actually migrated yet, since nothing verified the announcement actually worked
No risk — skipping monitoring has no effect if a sunset date was announced
The risk only applies to GraphQL fields, not REST endpoints
The risk is eliminated as long as the announcement was made in writing
items.explanation: Without monitoring, there's no way to know whether the announcement actually resulted in clients migrating — removing on schedule regardless of real usage is exactly how an announced date turns into a real outage.

items.prompt: What does "direct outreach to remaining callers" accomplish in the deprecation flow?
choices: It reaches clients who might have missed a general announcement, especially unattended or abandoned integrations
It's a purely ceremonial step with no effect on who actually migrates
It replaces the need for monitoring usage entirely
It's only relevant for internal clients, never external partners
items.explanation: A general announcement doesn't reach everyone — unattended scripts and abandoned integrations are exactly the kind of caller that needs a more direct nudge once monitoring reveals they're still active.

items.prompt: Is reaching a sunset date, by itself, sufficient justification to remove a deprecated field?
choices: No — the date is a target; usage still needs to be confirmed as actually gone first
Yes — the date is the only condition that matters
Yes, but only for fields deprecated for more than a year
No, because sunset dates are never actually enforced in practice
items.explanation: The date alone doesn't prove migration happened — it's the combination of a passed date and confirmed dropped usage that makes removal actually safe, not the date in isolation.

items.prompt: In the deprecation flow, what happens if usage monitoring after the announced sunset date still shows meaningful traffic?
choices: The flow loops back to notifying remaining callers directly, rather than removing on schedule regardless
The field is removed anyway, since the date has already passed
The announcement is cancelled and the field becomes permanent
The field is immediately un-deprecated
items.explanation: Nonzero usage after the sunset date is exactly the case the monitoring step is designed to catch — the appropriate response is more direct outreach, not proceeding with removal regardless of what the data shows.

items.prompt: handleV1Weather and handleV2Weather both call the same getWeatherReading and celsiusToFahrenheit functions, rather than each reimplementing the lookup and conversion. If celsiusToFahrenheit's rounding is later fixed, what happens to handleV1Weather's output?
choices: It picks up the fix automatically, since it calls the same function rather than its own copy of the math
Nothing changes, since handleV1Weather already computed its own independent result

It doesn't — v1 should return the raw celsius value directly without any conversion

Because celsiusToFahrenheit also updates the database as a side effect
