items.prompt: getWeatherReading(cityId) returns { celsius }. Both v1 and v2 adapters call it. Does getWeatherReading need to know which version is calling it?
choices: No — it's version-agnostic and just returns the reading; shaping the response for a specific version is the adapter's job
Yes — it must return a different shape depending on the caller's version
Yes, but only for v2, since v1 predates the versioning scheme
No, but only because celsius values never change
items.explanation: The shared core stays simple specifically because it doesn't need to know about versions at all — that knowledge belongs entirely in the thin adapters sitting on top of it.

items.prompt: If celsiusToFahrenheit(celsius) is called identically from both handleV1Weather and handleV2Weather, will it ever return two different results for the same celsius input?
choices: No — same function, same input, always the same output
Yes — it returns a different result depending on which adapter called it
Only if the adapters pass the cityId as well
Only for negative Celsius values
items.explanation: A pure shared function returns the same result for the same input regardless of caller — that consistency is exactly what keeps v1 and v2 from silently disagreeing about the same underlying value.

items.prompt: handleV2Weather returns both tempF and tempC. Should tempC be computed by a separate, independent lookup, or derived from the same celsius value used for tempF?
choices: Derived from the exact same celsius value already fetched, to guarantee tempF and tempC are always consistent with each other
A separate independent lookup, so a bug in one doesn't affect the other
It doesn't matter, since tempF and tempC are unrelated numbers
tempC should always be hardcoded, since it doesn't change often
items.explanation: Deriving both fields from the one celsius value already fetched guarantees they can never disagree with each other — a second, independent lookup would risk returning a different reading if anything changed between the two calls.

items.prompt: Which of these is a thin adapter's job, versus the shared core's job?
choices: Adapter: reshape the core's result into the version's response shape. Core: fetch and compute the underlying data
Adapter: fetch and compute the underlying data. Core: reshape it per version
Both the adapter and the core should independently fetch and compute the data
Neither — fetching, computing, and reshaping should all happen in the HTTP routing layer
items.explanation: The split is deliberate: the core does the real work (fetching, computing) exactly once, and each adapter's only job is translating that single result into its own version's shape.

items.prompt: A bug is found in getWeatherReading's lookup logic (wrong data for one city). Does fixing it require touching handleV1Weather or handleV2Weather?
choices: No — fixing getWeatherReading alone fixes the data both adapters receive
Yes — both adapters need the same fix applied to their own code
Only handleV2Weather needs the fix
Only handleV1Weather needs the fix, since v2 doesn't use getWeatherReading directly
items.explanation: Since both adapters call getWeatherReading rather than reimplementing the lookup, a fix made there alone is immediately visible to both — no adapter code needs to change.

items.prompt: Why does handleV1Weather "differ only in how it maps the core's result to JSON," rather than holding any lookup or conversion logic of its own?
choices: Because holding its own copy of that logic would duplicate what the shared core already does, risking the two drifting apart over time
Because v1 is not allowed to call any shared functions, by convention
Because JSON mapping is the only thing REST APIs are capable of doing
Because v1 predates the existence of a shared core
items.explanation: Keeping v1's adapter limited to reshaping, with zero independent logic, is exactly what prevents it from silently falling out of sync with v2 or with the core over time.

items.prompt: Suppose a third version, v3, needs a response shape like { tempKelvin }. Should v3's adapter reimplement a Celsius-to-Kelvin conversion from scratch, independent of the existing core?
choices: No — it should call the shared core to get the celsius reading, then do its own unit conversion as a thin adapter step, the same pattern v1/v2 already follow
Yes — every new version should have a fully independent implementation for safety
It depends on whether v3 is a major or minor version
v3 cannot be added without rewriting v1 and v2 first
items.explanation: The pattern generalizes directly: v3 is just another thin adapter on top of the same shared core, differing only in which unit conversion and which field names it exposes — no need to duplicate the underlying lookup.

items.prompt: A GraphQL schema has temperature (deprecated), tempF, and tempC. The resolver for temperature is implemented by calling the exact same conversion function tempF's resolver uses, from the same underlying reading. What does this guarantee?
choices: temperature and tempF will always agree with each other, since they're computed the same way from the same source data
temperature will always return null, marking it as unavailable
temperature will be computed once and then cached forever, never updating
Nothing is guaranteed — the two fields could still diverge at runtime
items.explanation: Deriving the deprecated field from the exact same computation and source data as its replacement is what guarantees the two can never silently disagree — an old client reading temperature gets a value that's provably consistent with tempF.
items.reflection: Keeping a deprecated field's resolver fully correct — not stubbed, not stale — for as long as anyone uses it is the same discipline as maintaining a legacy code path everyone "knows" is going away: it still has to behave correctly for real users today, not just eventually be removed. Where have you seen a "soon to be removed" piece of a system get neglected while it was still actually load-bearing?

items.prompt: A resolver for a deprecated field is changed to simply return a hardcoded placeholder value instead of computing the real result, with a comment saying "it's deprecated anyway." What's wrong with this, given what @deprecated actually means?
choices: It breaks every client still querying that field, since @deprecated never promised the field would stop being accurate — only that it's scheduled for eventual removal
Nothing is wrong — a hardcoded placeholder is the expected behavior for any deprecated field
It's only a problem if the field's type is a scalar rather than an object
It's correct, since hardcoding is faster than computing the real value
items.explanation: @deprecated is a notice about the future, not a license to degrade correctness now. Any client still genuinely depending on that field — and there often still is one — gets silently wrong data the moment the resolver stops computing a real answer, which is a regression, not a deprecation.
items.reflection: Keeping a deprecated field's resolver fully correct — not stubbed, not stale — for as long as anyone uses it is the same discipline as maintaining a legacy code path everyone "knows" is going away: it still has to behave correctly for real users today, not just eventually be removed. items.prompt: Six months after temperature is marked @deprecated, a new engineer adds a second new field, tempKelvin, computed from the same underlying reading. They write tempKelvin's resolver independently, re-deriving the Celsius value with its own separate lookup rather than reusing the existing reading fetch used by temperature/tempF/tempC. What risk does this introduce, and how does it relate to the deprecated field staying correct?
choices: If the independent lookup can ever return a different reading than the shared one (e.g. due to timing or a cache), tempKelvin could disagree with temperature/tempF/tempC even though all four describe the same moment — the deprecated field being "still correct" only holds relative to a single consistent source of truth
There's no risk — since temperature is deprecated, it's fine for new fields to be computed completely independently of it
The risk only exists if tempKelvin is also marked @deprecated
This is required, since deprecated and non-deprecated fields must always use separate data sources
items.explanation: Deriving every related field from one consistent fetch of the underlying reading is what keeps them all honest with each other, deprecated or not. A newly-added field that goes around that shared source reintroduces exactly the kind of inconsistency risk the single-source-of-truth pattern (seen earlier with the shared REST core) is meant to prevent — regardless of which fields happen to be marked deprecated.
items.reflection: Keeping a deprecated field's resolver fully correct — not stubbed, not stale — for as long as anyone uses it is the same discipline as maintaining a legacy code path everyone "knows" is going away: it still has to behave correctly for real users today, not just eventually be removed. Where have you seen a "soon to be removed" piece of a system get neglected while it was still actually load-bearing?

items.prompt: Is a deprecated GraphQL field's resolver allowed to stop computing a real value, since it's "going away eventually"?
choices: No — it must keep computing a correct value for as long as any client can still query it
Yes — deprecated fields are expected to return stale or placeholder data
Yes, but only after the announced sunset date
No, but only for fields of type Float
items.explanation: @deprecated is a notice, not a license to let correctness slip — the field has to keep behaving like a normal, correct field until it's actually removed.

items.prompt: A deprecated field temperature and its replacement tempF are both resolved using the same celsiusToFahrenheit function applied to the same reading. Could they ever return different values for the same request?
choices: No — identical computation from identical input always produces identical output
Yes — deprecated fields always lag behind their replacements by design
Only if the client queries them in a different order
Only if the schema was updated after the deprecation
items.explanation: Same function, same input, same output — computing both fields the same way from the same source is exactly what rules out them ever disagreeing.

items.prompt: What happens to a client's query the moment a deprecated field's resolver function is actually deleted (not just marked @deprecated)?
choices: The query fails for that field — this is the real removal, as opposed to the earlier announcement
Nothing — deleting a resolver has no runtime effect
The field automatically falls back to its replacement field's value
The entire schema becomes invalid and every query fails
items.explanation: Deleting the resolver is the actual act of removal — until that point the field was fully live, so this is the moment a still-dependent client's query actually breaks.

items.prompt: Why does a deprecated field's resolver typically call the same underlying computation as its replacement, rather than having its own separate implementation?
choices: To guarantee the two fields stay consistent with each other and both reflect real, current data
Because GraphQL requires deprecated fields to share code with their replacement
Because separate implementations would be rejected by schema validation
There's no particular reason — it's just a stylistic preference
items.explanation: Sharing the computation is what keeps the old and new field from silently drifting apart — the same reasoning as the shared-core pattern for REST adapters.

items.prompt: A deprecated distance field and its replacement distanceMiles both derive from the same underlying km value. If a bug in the km-to-miles conversion is fixed, does distance also get fixed automatically?
choices: Yes — as long as distance calls the same conversion function distanceMiles uses
No — distance is frozen the moment it's marked @deprecated
Only if distance is queried before distanceMiles in the same request
No, because deprecated fields can't receive bug fixes
items.explanation: There's nothing special that freezes a deprecated field — if it calls the same shared function as its replacement, a fix to that function benefits both fields identically.

items.prompt: Is it correct to think of a deprecated field as "already removed, just not literally deleted yet"?
choices: No — it's still a fully live, fully functional part of the schema until the resolver/field is actually deleted
Yes — that's exactly what @deprecated means at runtime
Yes, but only after the sunset date passes
It depends on whether the client checks for the deprecation warning
items.explanation: That mental model is exactly the mistake that leads to premature deletion — a deprecated field is still fully live and expected to behave correctly, right up until the actual removal.

items.prompt: A resolver for a non-deprecated field accidentally returns a hardcoded value instead of a computed one. Is this a different kind of bug than doing the same thing to a deprecated field?
choices: No — it's the same kind of correctness bug either way; deprecation status doesn't change what counts as a bug
Yes — hardcoding is only a bug for non-deprecated fields
Yes — hardcoding a deprecated field is actually the expected, correct behavior
No, but only because GraphQL treats all scalar fields identically
items.explanation: A field returning a wrong, hardcoded value instead of the real computed one is a correctness bug regardless of whether that field happens to be marked @deprecated — the deprecation label doesn't lower the bar for correctness.

items.prompt: A function compares a deployed schema { temperature, cityId } against a proposed schema { tempF, cityId }, and is designed to detect fields present in the deployed schema but missing from the proposed one. What does it report for this comparison?
choices: temperature was removed — it exists in the deployed schema but has no matching entry in the proposed one
tempF was removed, since it's a new, unfamiliar field name
Nothing — since cityId is unchanged, the schemas are considered equivalent
Both temperature and cityId were removed, since the schema changed at all
items.explanation: The check only walks fields that exist in the deployed schema and asks whether each still has a counterpart in the proposed one. temperature has no match in the proposed schema (tempF is a different key, not recognized as "the same field"), so it's flagged as removed — cityId has a match, so it's fine.
items.reflection: A function that walks every key in an old snapshot and checks whether it's still present in a new one is a pattern that generalizes well past API schemas — diffing two config files to catch a dropped setting, diffing a database migration's "before" and "after" column list, or diffing a CLI's old and new flag set before a release. Where else might a simple "what's missing now that used to be there" check have caught a problem earlier?

items.prompt: The same removed-field check is run on a proposed schema that only adds new optional fields, with every field from the deployed schema still present under its original name. What does the check report, and why does that matter for how aggressively it can be run?
choices: It reports nothing — since the check only walks fields present in the deployed schema, fields that only exist in the new one are never even inspected, so pure additions never trigger a false alarm
It reports every new field as a potential removal, requiring a human to double-check each one
It reports an error, since the check can't handle schemas of different sizes
It reports the new fields as "renamed," assuming every addition corresponds to some removed field
items.explanation: Because the check iterates only over the deployed schema's keys, a newly-added field in the proposed schema is never visited by the loop at all — it can't possibly be flagged. This is exactly what lets the check run on every PR automatically without producing false positives for ordinary, safe, additive growth.
items.reflection: A function that walks every key in an old snapshot and checks whether it's still present in a new one is a pattern that generalizes well past API schemas — diffing two config files to catch a dropped setting, diffing a database migration's "before" and "after" column list, or diffing a CLI's old and new flag set before a release. Where else might a simple "what's missing now that used to be there" check have caught a problem earlier?

items.prompt: A proposed schema renames a field from status to orderStatus, while also removing an unrelated, genuinely-unused internal debug field called _internalTrace that no client has ever been able to see or query. Should a removed-field check flag both, flag only one, or flag neither — and why?
choices: It should flag both as "removed," since the check can't distinguish a user-facing rename from an unused internal field going away — a human still has to judge whether each flagged removal is actually risky, the check only finds candidates
It should flag only status, since _internalTrace was never used by any client
It should flag neither, since both changes are ultimately safe in practice
It should flag only _internalTrace, since renames are never considered removals
items.explanation: The check's logic is purely structural — it has no way to know which fields real clients actually read, so it correctly flags every field missing from the proposed schema, including ones that turn out to be safe to lose. That's by design: the check surfaces candidates for a human (or usage data) to judge, it doesn't claim every flagged removal is actually dangerous in practice.
items.reflection: A function that walks every key in an old snapshot and checks whether it's still present in a new one is a pattern that generalizes well past API schemas — diffing two config files to catch a dropped setting, diffing a database migration's "before" and "after" column list, or diffing a CLI's old and new flag set before a release. Where else might a simple "what's missing now that used to be there" check have caught a problem earlier?

items.prompt: A removed-field check walks every field in the deployed schema. What does it check for each one?
choices: Whether that same field name still exists in the proposed schema
Whether that field's type has changed in the proposed schema
Whether that field is marked as required
Whether the proposed schema has more total fields than the deployed one
items.explanation: The check's one job for removal-detection is presence — does this deployed field still have a matching name in the proposed schema, or has it disappeared.

items.prompt: Deployed schema: { a, b, c }. Proposed schema: { a, b }. What does a removed-field check report?
choices: c was removed
a and b were removed
Nothing — since a and b are still present
d was removed
items.explanation: c is the only field present in the deployed schema with no counterpart in the proposed one, so it's exactly what gets flagged.

items.prompt: Deployed schema: { price, sku }. Proposed schema: { price, sku, discount }. What does a removed-field check report?
choices: Nothing — every deployed field still exists in the proposed schema; discount is a pure addition
discount was removed
price was removed
Both price and sku were removed, since a new field was added
items.explanation: Every field from the deployed schema (price, sku) is still present, so nothing is flagged — discount being new and additional doesn't register as a removal, since the check never inspects fields that only exist in the proposed side.

items.prompt: Why does a removed-field check only loop over the deployed schema's fields, rather than looping over the proposed schema's fields instead?
choices: Because "removed" is defined relative to what used to exist — looping over the old schema is what lets it find fields that disappeared
Looping over either schema produces identical results, so it doesn't matter
Looping over the proposed schema is actually required for correctness
Because the proposed schema is always smaller than the deployed one
items.explanation: Removal is inherently about what existed before and is now gone — the only way to find that is to check each field that used to be there, which means iterating the deployed (old) schema.

items.prompt: Deployed schema: { id, name, email }. Proposed schema: {}. What does a removed-field check report?
choices: id, name, and email were all removed
Nothing — an empty proposed schema can't be compared
Only id was removed
The check throws an error on an empty schema
items.explanation: Every field from the deployed schema is missing from the (empty) proposed schema, so all three — id, name, and email — are correctly flagged as removed.

items.prompt: A field is renamed from username to handle. From the removed-field check's point of view, what does this look like?
choices: username is reported as removed — the check has no concept of "rename," only presence/absence
The check recognizes it as a rename and reports no removal
handle is reported as removed, since it's the new, unrecognized name
Both usernam and handle are reported as removed
items.explanation: The check only compares field names for presence — it has no way to know handle is "the same concept" as username, so a rename shows up exactly like a removal, which is actually correct from an old client's point of view.

items.prompt: If a removed-field check reports an empty list for a given schema comparison, what does that tell you?
choices: Every field that existed in the deployed schema still exists, under the same name, in the proposed schema
The two schemas are byte-for-byte identical
No fields exist in either schema
The proposed schema has fewer fields than the deployed one
items.explanation: An empty result specifically means nothing from the old schema disappeared — it says nothing about whether new fields were added, since additions were never part of what this check is looking for.

items.prompt: A type-change check only compares fields present in BOTH the old and new schema, skipping any field that exists in just one side. For oldSchema = { id: 'string', age: 'number' } and newSchema = { id: 'string', age: 'string' }, what does it report?
choices: age changed from number to string — id is unchanged, and age exists in both schemas with a different type in each
id changed from string to number
Nothing, since newSchema has the same number of fields as oldSchema
Both id and age changed, since the schema changed at all
items.explanation: Only age exists in both schemas with mismatched types, so it's the one flagged. id is present in both with the identical type, so it's correctly left alone.
items.reflection: These two checks share one deeper idea: not every change to a shared field is equally dangerous, and the direction of a change matters as much as the fact that something changed. The same asymmetry shows up in a database column going from nullable to non-null, a function parameter gaining a non-optional argument, or a permission model tightening who's allowed to do something. Where have you seen "loosening is safe, tightening isn't" apply outside of API schemas?

items.prompt: A required-change check for oldSchema = { cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: false } } and newSchema = { cityId: { required: true }, notes: { required: true } } should only flag the direction that rejects requests old clients used to be able to send. What does it report?
choices: notes became required — it moved from optional to required, which rejects requests that used to succeed
cityId became required, since it's listed first
Both fields changed, since both appear in both schemas
Nothing, since cityId's required status didn't change
items.explanation: notes moved from required: false to required: true — exactly the unsafe, tightening direction the check is designed to catch. cityId's required status is unchanged (true to true), so it correctly isn't flagged.
items.reflection: These two checks share one deeper idea: not every change to a shared field is equally dangerous, and the direction of a change matters as much as the fact that something changed. The same asymmetry shows up in a database column going from nullable to non-null, a function parameter gaining a non-optional argument, or a permission model tightening who's allowed to do something. Where have you seen "loosening is safe, tightening isn't" apply outside of API schemas?

items.prompt: A proposed schema change makes a field go from required: true to required: false, AND separately changes that same field's type from 'string' to 'number'. Running both a type-change check and a required-change check against this proposal, what should happen?
choices: The type-change check flags the field (type changed, regardless of direction); the required-change check does NOT flag it, since required-to-optional is the safe, loosening direction — the two checks are independently judging two different, unrelated properties of the same field
Neither check flags anything, since loosening required status cancels out the type change
Both checks flag it, since any combination of changes to the same field is automatically unsafe
Only the required-change check flags it, since type changes are always considered safe by convention
items.explanation: The two checks test genuinely independent properties: a type change is unsafe in either direction (old parsing logic assumed one specific type), while a required-status change is only unsafe in the tightening direction. A field can trip one check without tripping the other — running both and reasoning about each on its own terms is exactly correct here, not a contradiction.
items.reflection: These two checks share one deeper idea: not every change to a shared field is equally dangerous, and the direction of a change matters as much as the fact that something changed. The same asymmetry shows up in a database column going from nullable to non-null, a function parameter gaining a non-optional argument, or a permission model tightening who's allowed to do something. Where have you seen "loosening is safe, tightening isn't" apply outside of API schemas?

items.prompt: A type-change check skips any field that only exists in one of the two schemas. Why?
choices: Because a field existing in only one schema is a removal or addition, a different category of change than "its type changed"
Because the check can't handle schemas of different sizes at all
Because such fields are always considered safe by definition
Because the check only works on schemas with identical field counts
items.explanation: "Type changed" only makes sense for a field present on both sides to compare — a field missing from one side belongs to the removal/addition category instead, which a separate check handles.

items.prompt: oldSchema = { total: 'number' }, newSchema = { total: 'number' }. What does a type-change check report?
choices: Nothing — the type is identical on both sides
total changed from number to number
An error, since nothing changed
total was removed
items.explanation: Identical types on both sides mean there's nothing to flag — the check only reports a difference, not every field it inspects.

items.prompt: A required-change check flags a field going from required: true to required: false. Is this the intended behavior?
choices: No — that direction loosens a constraint and can't break an old client, so it shouldn't be flagged
Yes — any change to required status should be flagged regardless of direction
Yes, because loosening a field is just as risky as tightening it
It depends on the field's type
items.explanation: Only the optional-to-required direction rejects requests that used to succeed. Flagging the opposite, safe direction would be a bug in the check, not correct behavior.

items.prompt: oldSchema = { email: { required: true } }, newSchema = { email: { required: true } }. What does a required-change check report?
choices: Nothing — required status is unchanged
email became required
email became optional
An error, since the schemas are identical
items.explanation: No change in required status means nothing for the check to report — it only flags the specific optional-to-required transition, which didn't happen here.

items.prompt: oldSchema = { quantity: 'number' }, newSchema = { quantity: 'string' }. What does a type-change check report?
choices: quantity changed from number to string
Nothing, since quantity exists in both schemas
quantity was removed and a new field was added
An error, since number and string are incompatible
items.explanation: quantity exists in both schemas but with different types, which is exactly the condition the check is designed to catch and report.

items.prompt: Why is a type change considered unsafe in either direction (number-to-string or string-to-number), unlike a required-status change which is only unsafe in one direction?
choices: Because old client code written to parse/use one type doesn't automatically work correctly against the other type, regardless of which direction the change goes
Because type changes are always reversible, unlike required-status changes
Because only number-to-string is actually unsafe; string-to-number is always fine
Because type changes only affect requests, never responses
items.explanation: Required/optional has a genuinely safe direction (loosening), but there's no equivalent "safe direction" for a type change — old code built around one type's behavior breaks regardless of which specific types are involved.

items.prompt: A required-change check and a type-change check are run against the same proposed schema change. Can a single field be flagged by one check but not the other?
choices: Yes — the two checks test different, independent properties of a field, so a field can trip one without tripping the other
No — any field flagged by one check must always be flagged by both
No, because the two checks are actually the same check with different names
Only if the field's type is a boolean
items.explanation: Type and required-status are separate properties of a field — a field can change one without the other, so the two checks can legitimately disagree about whether a given field is flagged.

items.prompt: A version-bump rule says: any breaking change forces MAJOR; otherwise any new field forces MINOR; otherwise PATCH. For a release with 1 breaking change and 0 new fields, what's the bump?
choices: MAJOR
MINOR
PATCH
It can't be determined without more information
items.explanation: The rule's precedence is breaking changes first — one is already present, which alone forces MAJOR regardless of how many (zero, here) additive changes also shipped.
items.reflection: Mapping a diff's findings to a single, predictable number — MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH — is what turns a one-off judgment call into something consumers can plan around automatically, the same role a changelog, a release-notes severity tag, or a dependency's semver range plays for any piece of software a team depends on. Where have you relied on a version number alone to decide whether an upgrade was safe to take automatically?

items.prompt: Using the same rule, a release has 0 breaking changes and 3 new optional fields. What's the bump?
choices: MINOR
MAJOR
PATCH
